result:
I'd pick **PostgreSQL**, with a `JSONB` column for the varying attributes.

A catalogue is only partly schemaless. Every product shares a core (SKU, name, price, category, stock, supplier) that is relational and benefits from constraints and joins, and only the long tail of attributes varies. Postgres handles both halves in one system, while MongoDB handles the variable half well and the relational half less well.

| Concern | PostgreSQL (+ JSONB) | MongoDB |
|---|---|---|
| Varied attributes | JSONB column, indexed with GIN; good, slightly clunkier query syntax | Native and most ergonomic |
| Shared core fields | Typed columns, foreign keys, check constraints | Enforced only through optional schema validation and application code |
| Relations (categories, variants, pricing, inventory, orders) | Joins and foreign keys | `$lookup` works but is awkward and slower; otherwise you denormalise and manage duplication |
| Transactions | Mature, cheap, default | Multi-document transactions exist but cost more and are not the usual pattern |
| Faceted filtering on arbitrary attributes | One GIN index covers containment queries; range queries on specific keys need expression indexes | Wildcard indexes are flexible; similar trade-offs for range queries |
| Reporting | Full SQL, wide tooling support | Aggregation pipeline is capable but less widely supported |
| Horizontal write scaling | Needs extra work (Citus, partitioning, application sharding) | Built-in sharding |
| Search | Built-in full-text is adequate; serious search needs a dedicated engine | Same, unless you use Atlas Search |

**Where Postgres costs you**
- Updating one key inside a JSONB value rewrites the whole value, which matters for large documents updated often.
- The planner has poor statistics on JSONB contents, so some attribute queries need hand-tuned indexes.
- Attributes you filter or sort on heavily should be promoted to real columns over time.

**When I would pick MongoDB instead**
- The catalogue is a mostly standalone, read-heavy store of deeply nested documents with few relations to other data.
- You expect write volume or data size that needs sharding from early on.
- The team already runs MongoDB well and has no Postgres experience.

Most catalogues do not meet those conditions: they are modest in size (millions of products fit comfortably on one Postgres node) and are tied closely to pricing, inventory and orders, where integrity matters more than schema flexibility.

If you tell me the expected product count, the write rate, and whether orders and inventory live in the same database, I can check that the recommendation still holds.
